newsitem.title: USA: NASA sees further delays by Russia on Space Station.
newsitem.headline: NASA sees further delays by Russia on Space Station.

text.p: NASA said on Wednesday that Russia's financial woes could further delay the planned International Space Station and said it was making costly contingency plans to go ahead on its own.

In testimony to a House of Representatives subcommittee on space, Wilbur Trafton, NASA's Associate Administrator of Space Flight, said Russia's space agency was in dire need of cash to build a critical service module.

Trafton told the panel that the Russian Space Agency needed 800 billion rubles (abuot $140 million) this month and next to pay its suppliers to keep the service module on schedule for launch in December 1998. Technical and money problems delayed the planned launch next spring.
The NASA official said the agency wants to take $200 million from the Space Shuttle budget to pay for contingency plans and an additional $100 million to help the Russian program.

"We have initiated a contingency plan to ensure that we can continue the ISS (International Space Station) assembly process despite the service module delays," he said. A previously secret U.S. Navy space vehicle could be ready for launch by late 1998, replacing the Russian service module, he said.
"We are going ahead," Trafton said. "We are saying to the Russians: 'Join us if and when you can.'"

House Science Committee chairman James Sensenbrenner, a Wisconsin Republican, said he did not believe NASA's assurance that the transfer of money would not harm the Space Shuttle program and said the Russian service module might not be ready until October 1999.
"I don't think the American people are at all prepared or willing to pay any price to keep Russia in the International Space Station program just to avoid wounding Russia's pride," he said.

The critical 20-tonne Russian service module was meant to be launched in time to help control the first major piece of the space station, the 21-tonne, 43-foot-long (13 metres) Functional Energy Block, procured by Boeing and to be launched by Russia, to supply power for the project.

Altogether, the space station will be about 175 yards (160 metres) long and weigh 460 tonnes to house U.S., Russian and other scientists starting with a target date of 2002 after other segments are put in place by a series of about 10 U.S. shuttle launches.

The Energy Block, which will be locked onto by other modules made by the two countries as well as in Europe and Japan, needs help in controlling and stabilizing itself as it orbits 220 miles (354 km) above the Earth, circling every 90 minutes.
There have been continuing delays in the space station project since former President Ronald Reagan first proposed it in 1984 "to follow our dreams to distant stars ..."
Russian and U.S. astronauts started in 1994 to rendevous with the Russian space station Mir as a prelude to the far more complex International Space Station.
On Tuesday an unmanned Russian cargo craft docked with Mir to bring oxygen reserves and equipment to two Russian cosmonauts and a U.S. astronaut to help them repair their air supply system.

The latest in a series of problems in Russia's cash-strapped space program prompted a NASA official to say the U.S. space agency would review safety on Mir before sending any more astronauts to live and work there.
